title: The last confession
hook: a short prayer of confession said near death

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was visiting lightens: Akiva at the bedside of a student nobody else came to see. Today we stay at the bedside, for the hardest conversation there is.

How do you tell someone who is very sick that it might be time to make their peace, without telling them they're dying? Jewish tradition has a sentence ready, and it's a strange, kind one. Before the confession, the visitor says something like: many have confessed and not died, and many have not confessed and died. Saying this prayer is not a verdict. It doesn't summon anything. It's simply good to be ready.
screen: `THE HARDEST CONVERSATION.` → `CONFESSING IS NOT A VERDICT.` → `IT'S GOOD TO BE READY.`

segments.voice: The prayer is vidui, confession, a word you met in your second year. The same word names the confession said on Yom Kippur, when a whole congregation admits its wrongs together. This one is said alone, or with a few people close by, near the end of life. The Talmud teaches that when a person falls ill and is close to death, they are told: confess. It's not a punishment. The Mishnah teaches that whoever confesses has a share in the world to come. Confession is a door, not a sentence. And it's gentle. The codes say not to raise it in front of people who will break down crying, so the sick person isn't frightened. If they can't speak, they can confess in their heart. If they can't manage the full text, a few words are enough. The tradition bends toward the person in the bed. Wordings vary, but the short vidui acknowledges that healing and death are both in God's hands, asks for healing if it can be, asks that if death comes it be counted as atonement for wrongs done, and asks for care for the family left behind. It's honest about both outcomes at once. Traditionally, the last words are the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. The line from childhood bedtime becomes the last line of all. Vidui isn't about fear. It's about not leaving the important things unsaid.
screen: `THEY TELL HIM: CONFESS.` · `GENTLE, NEVER FRIGHTENING.` · `HONEST ABOUT BOTH OUTCOMES.` · `IT ENDS WITH THE SHEMA.` · then, large: `READY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself one quiet question, nothing morbid: if today were my last, what would I wish I'd said? Let one thing come, an apology owed, a thank-you never sent, an I love you, and breathe with it; if you pray, you can say the Shema slowly, or sit in silence. If thoughts of death ever feel heavy rather than gentle, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Vidui. Confession: said near the end of life, gently, honest about healing and death, and closing with the Shema. Today's word.
Your line: ready. Nothing important left unsaid, to anyone you love. Go gently.

howItsDone: When a Jew is gravely ill, a family member, friend or rabbi may gently offer to say the vidui with them, a short confession found in prayer books; it is often followed by the Shema.

chat.who: a friend who volunteers at a hospital
chat.says: Doesn't saying the vidui mean you're telling someone they're about to die?
options: No; it starts with: many have confessed and not died. It's about being ready.
Yes; the prayer asks God to take the person, so it's said only at the end.
Yes, which is why it's always kept secret from the person who is sick.
